1896–1934 · USSR

Lev Vygotski

Soviet psychologist who argued for the social and cultural origin of the mind. He proposed that we learn with the help of others and of tools such as language, and formulated the zone of proximal development.

Biography

Lev Semyonovich Vygotsky was born in 1896 in Orsha, in present-day Belarus, and grew up in Gomel in a cultured Jewish family. He studied law at Moscow University and, at the same time, history and philosophy at the Shanyavsky People's University. After the revolution he taught in Gomel, where he became interested in psychology and education.

In 1924 he gave a talk at a congress in Leningrad that made such an impression that he was invited to work at the Institute of Psychology in Moscow. In barely ten years he wrote an enormous body of work, despite suffering from tuberculosis. He died in 1934, aged 37.

Questions he investigated

  • How are basic mental capacities transformed into higher forms, such as voluntary memory or abstract thought?
  • What role do language and culture play in the development of thinking?
  • How can children best be helped to learn, including those with disabilities?

Contributions

Vygotsky proposed that higher mental functions have a social origin: they first appear between people and are then internalised. A child learns to guide their own behaviour because adults have first guided it with words. For him, the mind is mediated by cultural tools, above all language, just as work is mediated by physical tools.

His best-known concept is the zone of proximal development: the distance between what a child can do alone and what they can do with help from an adult or a more capable peer. Good teaching, he said, is aimed at that zone. He also studied inner speech: the child who talks aloud while playing is learning to use language to think.

Collaborations, influences and disagreements

He worked with Alexander Luria and Alexei Leontiev, with whom he formed the so-called troika of the cultural-historical school. He disputed Jean Piaget's ideas about egocentric speech: Piaget saw it as a sign of the child's immaturity, Vygotsky as a step towards verbal thought. Piaget read his critique decades later and responded respectfully.

A documented anecdote

Two years after his death, a 1936 decree against "pedology", the study of the child then practised in the USSR, meant his work stopped being published for two decades. It was rescued in the late 1950s, and the 1962 English translation of Thought and Language made him known in the West, almost thirty years after his death.

Criticism, limits and reception

Vygotsky left many ideas sketched out and little developed empirically, and some of his texts were published with editors' changes. Historians still debate exactly what he said. His influence on education is enormous: cooperative learning, the "scaffolding" later proposed by Wood, Bruner and Ross, and attention to the cultural context of development owe much to his ideas.

References

  1. Vygotsky, L. S. (1978). Mind in society: The development of higher psychological processes. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press.
  2. Vygotsky, L. S. (1986). Thought and language (trad. A. Kozulin). Cambridge, MA: MIT Press. (Orig. ruso, 1934).
  3. Van der Veer, R. y Valsiner, J. (1991). Understanding Vygotsky: A quest for synthesis. Oxford: Blackwell.
